title: Azure AI Fundamentals
subtitle: 20 questions across AI workloads, machine learning, computer vision, NLP, and generative AI

gradeLabels.f: F-RANK -- Back to the Training Data

questions.q: A hospital system uses an AI model to predict patient readmission risk from historical records. Which AI workload category best describes this?
questions.note: Predictive analytics uses historical data and ML models to forecast future outcomes. Readmission risk scoring is a classic supervised regression or classification task under this workload category.

explain.correct: Predictive analytics applies ML to historical data to forecast future events — readmission risk is exactly this pattern.
wrong: NLP processes text or speech; historical patient records used for risk scoring is not primarily a text-understanding task.
Computer vision processes images and video; this scenario involves structured tabular records, not image data.
Generative AI produces new content such as text or images; risk prediction is discriminative, not generative.

questions.q: An AI hiring tool consistently ranks candidates from certain zip codes lower than equally qualified candidates from other areas. Which Responsible AI principle is being violated?
questions.note: Fairness requires that AI systems treat all people equitably and do not encode or amplify discriminatory biases. Zip-code-based disparate outcomes are a textbook fairness violation.

explain.correct: Fairness means AI must not discriminate against individuals or groups based on characteristics like location or demographics.
wrong: Reliability & Safety concerns whether the system performs correctly and safely under expected and unexpected conditions — not bias against groups.
Privacy & Security concerns protecting personal data from unauthorized access or misuse — not differential treatment by group.
Inclusiveness is about ensuring AI benefits everyone, including marginalized groups, but the specific principle violated by biased scoring is Fairness.

questions.q: A financial firm wants to ensure users can understand why their loan application was denied by an AI model. Which Responsible AI principle guides this requirement?
questions.note: Transparency requires that AI systems and their decisions be understandable and explainable to the people they affect. Being able to explain a loan denial directly maps to this principle.

explain.correct: Transparency means making AI systems and their decision logic understandable — explaining why a decision was made satisfies this principle.
wrong: Accountability is about ensuring humans remain responsible for AI decisions and can be held answerable — it does not directly address explainability to end users.
Fairness is about avoiding bias and discriminatory outcomes — it is about equitable treatment, not about explaining individual decisions.
Reliability & Safety is about ensuring the system works as intended consistently — not about decision explainability.

questions.q: A dataset of 10,000 house sales includes square footage, number of bedrooms, and final sale price. A model is trained to predict the sale price of new houses. What type of machine learning is this?
questions.note: Supervised learning uses labeled training data — each house record has a known sale price (the label). The model learns the mapping from features to label to make predictions on new data.

explain.correct: Supervised learning trains on labeled examples; the known sale price is the label, and the model learns to predict it from input features.
wrong: Unsupervised learning has no labels — it discovers patterns in unlabeled data. Sale price is a provided label here.
Reinforcement learning trains an agent through rewards and penalties for actions in an environment — it is not used for this kind of price prediction.
Clustering is an unsupervised technique that groups similar records — it does not predict a numeric output like sale price.

questions.q: Which machine learning task predicts a continuous numeric output, such as tomorrow's temperature?
questions.note: Regression predicts a continuous numeric value. Classification predicts a discrete category. Temperature is a continuous number, making regression the correct task type.

explain.correct: Regression maps input features to a continuous numeric output — predicting a temperature value is a canonical regression problem.
wrong: Classification predicts a discrete category label (e.g., hot/cold/mild), not a continuous number.
Clustering is an unsupervised method that groups similar data points — it does not produce a numeric prediction for a new input.
Segmentation assigns a class label to each pixel in an image (computer vision) — it is unrelated to numeric prediction.

questions.q: A retailer groups its customers into segments by purchasing behavior without using any pre-assigned labels. Which ML technique is being used?
questions.note: Clustering is an unsupervised ML technique that discovers natural groupings in unlabeled data. No predefined category labels are required — the algorithm identifies structure from the data itself.

explain.correct: Clustering finds natural groupings in unlabeled data — customer segmentation by behavior is the classic clustering use case.
wrong: Regression predicts a continuous numeric value from labeled training data — not applicable to grouping unlabeled customers.
Supervised classification requires labeled training examples for each class — the scenario explicitly has no pre-assigned labels.
Reinforcement learning trains an agent via environmental rewards — it is not used for grouping static customer records.

questions.q: After training a binary classifier, the model correctly identifies 90 out of 100 actual positive cases but also incorrectly flags 40 negative cases as positive. What is the model's recall?
questions.note: Recall = TP / (TP + FN). With 90 true positives and 10 false negatives (100 actual positives total), recall = 90/100 = 90%. Precision would be 90/130 ≈ 69%.

explain.correct: Recall = TP / (TP + FN) = 90 / (90 + 10) = 90%. It measures how many actual positives the model correctly found.
wrong: 69% is the precision (TP / (TP + FP) = 90 / 130), not the recall. Precision and recall measure different error directions.
56% is not a correct result for either recall or precision given these numbers.
82% is not a correct result for either recall or precision given these numbers.

questions.q: A data scientist wants to build an ML pipeline without writing code by connecting pre-built component tiles in a visual canvas on Azure Machine Learning. Which tool does this describe?
questions.note: Azure Machine Learning Designer is the no-code drag-and-drop visual canvas where users connect dataset, transform, and model tiles to build pipelines. AutoML automates algorithm selection but requires supplying a dataset and target column, not visual pipeline construction.

explain.correct: Azure ML Designer is the drag-and-drop graphical pipeline builder inside Azure Machine Learning — it requires no code.
wrong: Azure AutoML automates algorithm and hyperparameter selection given a dataset and label column — the user does not visually connect pipeline tiles.
Azure AI Studio is a portal for building generative AI and copilot solutions — it is not the no-code ML pipeline canvas.
Azure Databricks is a big-data analytics platform built on Apache Spark — it is code-centric and not part of the Azure ML Designer experience.

questions.q: Which metric best measures the proportion of all predicted positive results that are actually correct?
questions.note: Precision = TP / (TP + FP). It answers: of everything the model labeled positive, what fraction was truly positive? Recall instead measures what fraction of actual positives were found.

explain.correct: Precision = TP / (TP + FP) — it quantifies the trustworthiness of positive predictions, penalizing false positives.
wrong: Recall = TP / (TP + FN) — it measures how many of the actual positives were caught, not the correctness of positive predictions.
Accuracy = (TP + TN) / total — it measures overall correctness across all classes, not specifically the quality of positive predictions.
F1 Score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall — it balances both but is not purely a measure of positive prediction correctness.

questions.q: Which Azure Computer Vision task draws a rectangular bounding box around each detected object and returns its class label?
questions.note: Object detection locates individual objects in an image and returns both a class label and a bounding box for each. Image classification assigns a single label to the entire image.

explain.correct: Object detection identifies where objects are (bounding boxes) AND what they are (class labels) — both outputs together define detection.
wrong: Image classification assigns one label to the entire image without locating individual objects.
Semantic segmentation classifies every pixel in the image — it is more granular than bounding boxes.
Optical character recognition extracts printed or handwritten text from images — it does not detect general object classes.

questions.q: A developer wants to train a custom model to identify specific company logos in product photos, without writing ML code. Which Azure service is designed for this?
questions.note: Azure Custom Vision allows developers to upload labeled images, train a custom image classification or object detection model through a point-and-click portal, and publish a prediction endpoint — no ML code required.

explain.correct: Azure Custom Vision is purpose-built for training custom image classification and object detection models with no-code tooling.
wrong: Azure AI Vision provides prebuilt, Microsoft-trained models — it cannot be trained on your own specific logo images.
Azure AI Document Intelligence extracts structured data from forms and documents — it is not used for training image classifiers.
Azure Machine Learning Designer builds ML pipelines through a drag-and-drop canvas but requires deeper ML knowledge and more setup than Custom Vision.

questions.q: A security system must determine whether any faces appear in a surveillance image. Which computer vision capability does this use?
questions.note: Facial detection locates and returns bounding boxes for any face regions in an image without identifying who those faces belong to. Facial recognition goes further by matching detected faces to known identities.

explain.correct: Facial detection finds the presence and location of faces in an image — it does not identify who the people are.
wrong: Facial recognition identifies WHO a detected face belongs to by comparing it to a known database of identities — more than locating faces.
Image classification assigns a single whole-image label — it would not pinpoint individual face regions.
Object segmentation classifies pixels — it does not specifically locate and label face regions as a dedicated capability.

questions.q: Which Azure AI Language feature identifies mentions of people, places, organizations, and dates within a block of text?
questions.note: Named Entity Recognition (NER) scans text and tags spans as named entities such as Person, Location, Organization, or DateTime. Sentiment analysis returns an overall positive/negative/neutral score.

explain.correct: NER identifies and classifies named entities (people, places, organizations, dates) as specific labeled spans within text.
wrong: Sentiment analysis returns a positive, negative, or neutral score for the overall tone of text — it does not extract named entity spans.
Key phrase extraction returns the main topics or concepts discussed in text — not specifically people, places, or organizations with typed labels.
Language detection identifies what language the text is written in — it does not extract entities.

questions.q: A customer service app must route incoming text messages to the correct support queue by understanding what the user wants to do. Which Azure AI Language feature handles this?
questions.note: CLU (Conversational Language Understanding) classifies user utterances into intents (e.g., 'CheckOrderStatus', 'RequestRefund') and extracts entities (e.g., order number). Intent classification is the primary feature used for routing.

explain.correct: CLU intent classification maps a user utterance to a predefined intent category — exactly what is needed to route messages to the correct queue.
wrong: Sentiment analysis scores the emotional tone of text — it does not determine what action the user wants to take.
Key phrase extraction identifies important topics but does not classify the user's goal into a named routing category.
NER extracts entity spans such as names and dates — it identifies what things are mentioned, not what the user intends to do.

questions.q: Which Azure AI service converts spoken audio into written text in real time?
questions.note: Azure AI Speech provides Speech-to-Text (STT) and Text-to-Speech (TTS) capabilities. STT transcribes spoken audio into text in real time or from recorded files. Azure AI Translator handles text-to-text translation across languages.

explain.correct: Azure AI Speech's Speech-to-Text feature transcribes spoken audio to written text, supporting real-time and batch scenarios.
wrong: Azure AI Translator converts text from one language to another — it processes text, not audio.
Azure AI Language analyzes and understands text (sentiment, NER, CLU) — it does not accept audio input directly.
Azure AI Vision analyzes images and video — it does not process audio streams.

questions.q: Large language models generate responses by doing which of the following?
options: Searching the internet for the most recent answer
Predicting the most probable next token given the preceding context
Retrieving answers from a structured database
questions.note: LLMs are trained to predict the next token in a sequence based on prior context. This autoregressive process, repeated token by token, produces fluent text. LLMs do not retrieve from databases or search the web unless augmented with tools.

explain.correct: LLMs work by predicting the next token (a word fragment, roughly 0.75 words) given all preceding tokens — this is autoregressive generation.
wrong: Base LLMs do not search the internet; that capability requires external tool augmentation such as Bing grounding in Azure OpenAI.
LLMs do not query structured databases — they generate responses from learned statistical patterns in weights.
LLMs use probabilistic neural networks, not deterministic rule trees — their outputs are stochastic, not rule-derived.

questions.q: An LLM confidently states that a fictional legal case is real and cites plausible-sounding but invented case numbers. What AI phenomenon does this illustrate?
questions.note: Hallucination occurs when an LLM generates plausible-sounding but factually incorrect or entirely fabricated information. It is a known limitation of generative AI that Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and grounding help mitigate.

explain.correct: Hallucination is when the model generates confident, fluent, but false content — fabricating case numbers and citations is a classic example.
wrong: Prompt injection is an attack where malicious instructions in the input override the intended system prompt — unrelated to generating false facts.
Grounding is the technique used to REDUCE hallucination by anchoring the model to verified external data sources.
Fine-tuning adapts a base model on domain-specific data — it is a training technique, not the phenomenon of generating false information.

questions.q: A developer provides three worked examples of the desired input-output format directly in the prompt before asking the model to handle a new input. Which prompting technique is this?
questions.note: Few-shot prompting includes a small number of example input-output pairs in the prompt to demonstrate the expected format or behavior. Zero-shot prompting provides no examples; chain-of-thought asks the model to reason step by step.

explain.correct: Few-shot prompting provides a small set of labeled examples in the prompt to guide the model's output format or reasoning style.
wrong: Zero-shot prompting asks the model to complete a task with no examples in the prompt — the model relies entirely on pretrained knowledge.
Chain-of-thought prompting instructs the model to show its reasoning steps before reaching a conclusion — it is about eliciting step-by-step reasoning, not providing examples.
System prompting sets the model's role or behavioral constraints via a system message — it does not describe providing worked examples in the user turn.

questions.q: Which Azure service provides access to OpenAI models such as GPT-4, DALL-E, and Whisper with enterprise security and compliance controls?
questions.note: Azure OpenAI Service is Microsoft's managed offering that provides access to OpenAI's foundation models (GPT-4, DALL-E 3, Whisper, embeddings) with Azure's enterprise-grade security, private networking, and compliance features.

explain.correct: Azure OpenAI Service is the specific Azure offering that hosts OpenAI models (GPT-4, DALL-E, Whisper) with enterprise controls.
wrong: Azure AI Studio is a unified portal for building AI applications — it uses Azure OpenAI Service under the hood but is not itself the service providing the models.
Azure Cognitive Services is an older umbrella brand; it has been reorganized into Azure AI Services — it is not the branded offering for GPT-4 and DALL-E.
Azure Machine Learning is for building and managing custom ML pipelines and models — it does not host OpenAI foundation models.

questions.q: A finance company needs to automatically extract vendor names, invoice totals, and line items from thousands of scanned PDF invoices. Which Azure AI service is purpose-built for this?
questions.note: Azure AI Document Intelligence (formerly Form Recognizer) extracts structured key-value pairs, tables, and fields from forms, invoices, and receipts using prebuilt or custom models. Plain OCR returns raw text without structured field extraction.

explain.correct: Azure AI Document Intelligence is purpose-built to extract structured data (fields, tables, key-value pairs) from forms and documents like invoices.
wrong: Azure AI Vision's Read OCR extracts raw text from images but does not understand document structure, field names, or invoice schema.
Azure AI Language NER identifies entity types in free text — it cannot reliably extract structured fields and totals from invoices at scale.
Azure Anomaly Detector detects outliers in time-series data — it has no capability to process documents or extract fields.
